# Dealing with Aluminium Oxidation on Body Panels

Steel rust and aluminium oxidation are fundamentally different phenomena, and treating them requires a complete shift in strategy. When you encounter bubbling paint on a steel car, the process is fairly standardized: sand back to bare metal, apply a chemical inhibitor like Krust to stop propagation, then fill and repaint. Aluminium, however, does not rust in the same way iron does, but it suffers from galvanic corrosion and surface oxidation that behaves differently under the clear coat.

The core issue with aluminium is that the oxide layer forms almost instantly upon exposure to air. While this native oxide layer actually protects the metal from further degradation in many industrial environments, on a car body panel, the chemistry is less forgiving. When a stone chip breaches the paint and primer, the underlying aluminium reacts with oxygen and moisture. Unlike steel rust, which is expansive and flakes off easily causing deep pits, aluminium corrosion often remains localized but can spread laterally if not addressed chemically before mechanical work begins.

Before you attempt to fill or repaint, you must neutralize the active corrosion. Simply sanding down bubbling aluminium paint often exposes fresh, reactive metal that will oxidize rapidly during the prep process, leading to new failures once the clear coat is applied. The standard approach involves using a dedicated aluminium treatment rather than generic rust inhibitors. Products specifically formulated for aluminium can help stabilize the surface and prevent the galvanic reaction from eating into the surrounding unpainted panels.

If you are working on a specific panel like a bonnet with multiple stone chips, consider the extent of the damage carefully. If the corrosion has penetrated deeply enough to create significant bubbling, sanding back to bare metal is necessary. However, unlike steel, where you might find deep cavities, aluminium oxidation tends to stay relatively shallow unless the structural integrity is compromised. You must ensure that all loose paint and oxidized layers are removed down to a bright, clean surface before applying any treatment.

Once the area is clean, apply your chosen aluminium-specific inhibitor according to the manufacturer's instructions. This step is critical because it creates a barrier that halts the electrochemical reaction. After treating the surface, you can proceed with filling and painting as usual. It is important to note that using steel-specific rust converters on aluminium is generally ineffective and can sometimes damage the finish or fail to stop the corrosion entirely.

The decision to replace a panel versus repairing it also depends on the severity of the oxidation. If the bubbling indicates widespread delamination, replacement might be more cost-effective than risking future corrosion issues. Always inspect the edges of the chip; if you see green or white powder underneath the paint, that is aluminium oxide, which requires immediate chemical intervention before any mechanical repair work begins.

The key takeaway is that patience during the cleaning and treating phase prevents costly mistakes down the line.
